title: In praise of boredom
summary_es: Una defensa del aburrimiento. Matices entre palabras casi sinónimas y expresiones idiomáticas.
text: Boredom has few defenders. We go to extraordinary {{1}} to avoid it, filling every idle moment with a screen, and we regard a bored child as a problem to be {{2}} rather than a normal state of affairs. Yet a growing body of research suggests that this aversion may be {{3}}. Boredom, on this view, is not an absence of stimulation so much as a signal that our current activity has ceased to be meaningful, and as such it {{4}} us to look for something that is. Deprived of that signal, we lose a powerful {{5}} for change. Novelists and composers have long {{6}} to the creative value of empty hours, and experiments now bear them {{7}}: participants set a tedious task subsequently generate more original ideas than those who were kept entertained. None of this is to romanticise tedium, which in its chronic form is closely {{8}} with depression. But the occasional dull afternoon may be precisely what an overstimulated mind requires.

gaps.explanation_es: «Go to great / extraordinary lengths to do something» = hacer lo indecible por.
Un problema se «arregla» con fix. «Heal» es para heridas, y «mend» y «repair», para objetos.
«Misplaced» se dice de un sentimiento dirigido a lo que no lo merece: misplaced fear, trust, loyalty. «Mislaid» es haber perdido un objeto.
«Prompt someone to do something» = impulsar a alguien a hacer algo. Los otros tres no admiten esa estructura.
«An impetus for change» = un estímulo para el cambio. «Momentum» es incontable y no admite «a».
«Attest to something» = dar fe de algo. «Vouch» va con for, y «confirm» y «assert» no llevan preposición.
«Bear someone out» = darle la razón, confirmar lo que dice.
«Closely associated with». «Related» y «attached» van con to.
